# 7.1 Sensitivity Analysis, Scenario Analysis, and Break-Even Analysis

## Sensitivity Analysis and Scenario Analysis

The net present value technique is used to determine whether a project should
be accepted. If the project's NPV is positive, the project should be accepted.
Otherwise it should be rejected. When calculating the NPV, you need to
understand which variables matter the most and how varying them will effect the
NPV. Two ways of studying the effects of the variables on NPV are Sensitivity
analysis and scenario analysis.

Sensitivity analysis allows you to vary one variable from a base case. The
advantage of this analysis is that you can observe how much impact a single
variable has on the NPV. The disadvantage to sensitivity analysis is that, in
the real world, most of the variables are related and vary together.

In the book, SEC sells solar-powered engines. SEC identifies the following
variables in its estimates of the revenues and costs used in calculating the
NPV.

* Market size (per year)
* Market share
* Price
* Variable cost (per plane)
* Fixed cost (per year)
* Investment

SEC's revenues and costs are calculated using these variables whereby the cash
flow and finally the NPV is calculated. The book outlines three scenarios for
each variable: the pessimistic, base, and optimistic. Then, the NPV is
calculated by varying one variable at a time and keeping the other variables at
base. Using this method it becomes obvious that the two variables that matter
most are market size and market share. When either of these variables are set
to the pessimistic value, the NPV turns negative. All other variables in the
pessimistic side, when used, keep the NPV positive. 

Scenario analysis allows you to set up more realistic scenarios. Here, instead
of testing each individual variable, you set up an event or story that explains
the environment you are making your decision in. The scenario will influence
how a set of variables will behave because they are related. This is in
contrast to sensitivity analysis where only one variable is changed at a time.
For example, the SEC plane crash scenario varies the market size and market
share variables because, in the event of a plane crash, travellers will be more
reluctant to use plane transportation. Also, because the solar-powered engine
technology is new, they will be more reluctant to use airplanes utilizing it.
This decreases the values of both variables which have already been shown to be
the most influencial variables for the NPV of the project. Because both
variables have dropped together, the value of the NPV is more negative than
when either of the variables drop individually.

Sensitivity analysis and scenario analysis are merely diagnostic tools. They do
not give a decision rule or probabilities for each scenario value.
